title: Characteristic‐Aligned Control‐Volume Physics‐Informed Neural Network for Flood‐Wave Propagation and Roughness Estimation
content:
Abstract

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a promising framework for river hydrodynamic simulation and parameter inversion under sparse observations. However, spatial heterogeneity in channel geometry and roughness causes strong variations in flood-wave propagation and parameter sensitivity, challenging local conservation and joint state-parameter estimation. This study proposes a Characteristic-aligned Control-volume Physics-Informed Neural Network for Roughness Estimation (CC-PINN-RE). It constructs dynamic diamond-shaped space-time control volumes from local characteristic speeds of the Saint-Venant equations, enforces mass and momentum conservation in integral form, and combines adaptive control-volume management with local-sensitivity-weighted roughness regularization. The method is evaluated on three one-dimensional channel cases of increasing complexity against strong-form PINN-RE and fixed-control-volume cvPINN-RE. CC-PINN-RE achieves the lowest errors in eight of nine relative L2 ${L}_{2}$ metrics for water depth, discharge, and roughness. In Case 3, where channel width, bed slope, and roughness vary spatially, it reduces the corresponding errors by 57.0%, 82.2%, and 57.3% relative to PINN-RE and reduces the maximum absolute error in peak water depth by 69.7%. Ablation experiments with three random seeds support the contributions of the three proposed components. Observation-deployment experiments show that increasing the number of monitoring stations is generally more effective than increasing temporal sampling frequency at individual stations. Under 0%–2% observational noise in Case 3, the model remains stable. These results indicate that CC-PINN-RE provides a physically consistent framework for integrating characteristic propagation, local conservation, and parameter inversion, offering a useful basis for joint hydrodynamic reconstruction and spatially varying roughness estimation in heterogeneous river channels.
